name: Fundamental Physics 1
description: Mechanics and Thermodynamics (EP7 Oscillations, EP8 Waves, EP9 Fluid Mechanics, EP10 Thermodynamics)

topics.title: Oscillations
topics.summary: Covers periodic motion and simple harmonic motion (SHM), where restoring force and acceleration are proportional and opposite to displacement. Encompasses kinematics and phase of mass-spring systems, mechanical energy conservation between kinetic and elastic potential energy, small-angle simple and physical pendulums (including tuned mass dampers), damped oscillations across underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped regimes, and forced oscillations with resonance.
keyPoints: Period $T$ and frequency $f = 1/T$ describe repetitive motion, with $1\text{ Hz} = 1\text{ cycle/s} = 1\text{ s}^{-1}$ and angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$.
In Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM), the net restoring force obeys $F_x = -kx$, giving the differential equation $d^2x/dt^2 = -(k/m)x = -\omega^2 x$.

SHM solutions $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$, $v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi)$, and $a(t) = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ have maxima $|v_{\max}| = A\omega$ at $x = 0$ and $|a_{\max}| = A\omega^2$ at $x = \pm A$.
For an ideal mass-spring oscillator, $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, independent of amplitude $A$.
Total mechanical energy in undamped SHM is conserved: $E_{\text{Total}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2$.

For small angles ($\sin\theta \approx \theta$), a simple pendulum has $\omega = \sqrt{g/L}$ (independent of mass), while a physical pendulum has $\omega = \sqrt{mgL/I}$ where $L$ is the distance from the pivot to the center of mass.

Linear viscous damping $F_D = -bv$ yields $x(t) = A_0 e^{-(b/2m)t}\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ with reduced frequency $\omega = \sqrt{k/m - (b/2m)^2}$ and three regimes: underdamped ($b^2 < 4mk$), critically damped ($b^2 = 4mk$), and overdamped ($b^2 > 4mk$).

Driven damped oscillators oscillate at the driving frequency $\omega$ with steady-state amplitude peaking near $\omega \approx \omega_0$ (resonance); heavier damping lowers and broadens the resonance peak.

topics.title: Waves
topics.summary: Covers mechanical traveling waves (transverse and longitudinal), sinusoidal wave equations, wave speed on a stretched string and in fluids, wave energy, average power, spherical intensity, superposition and phase-shifted interference, standing waves and normal modes on a string, beats, the Doppler effect, and shock waves (Mach cone and Cerenkov radiation).
keyPoints: Wave speed $v = \lambda / T = \lambda f = \omega / k$ is set by the medium ($v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$ on a string; $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ in a fluid), whereas frequency $f$ is set by the wave source.

In $y(x, t) = A\sin(kx \mp \omega t + \phi)$, $kx - \omega t$ propagates in the $+x$-direction and $kx + \omega t$ propagates in the $-x$-direction; maximum transverse particle speed is $v_{y,\max} = A\omega$.

Total mechanical energy per wavelength is split equally between kinetic and potential energy ($K_\lambda = U_\lambda = \frac{1}{4}\mu A^2\omega^2\lambda$), giving average power $P_{\text{ave}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu A^2\omega^2 v \propto A^2 f^2$.
Spherical wave intensity obeys the inverse-square law $I = P / (4\pi r^2) \propto 1/r^2$, meaning wave amplitude decays as $1/r$.

Two identical phase-shifted waves superimpose to $y_R(x, t) = [2A\cos(\phi/2)]\sin(kx - \omega t + \phi/2)$: constructive interference occurs at $\phi = 2m\pi$ ($A_R = 2A$) and destructive interference at $\phi = (2m+1)\pi$ ($A_R = 0$).

Opposing identical waves form a standing wave $y(x, t) = [2A\sin(kx)]\cos(\omega t)$ with adjacent nodes spaced by $\lambda/2$; symmetric fixed-end boundary conditions yield normal modes $\lambda_n = 2L/n$ and $f_n = n(v/2L) = nf_1$.
Beats arise from two close frequencies superimposing to produce an amplitude envelope varying at $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_2 - f_1|$ around carrier frequency $f_{\text{avg}} = (f_1 + f_2)/2$.

Doppler shift $f_o = f_s\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$ uses top signs ($+v_o, -v_s$) for approach and bottom signs ($-v_o, +v_s$) for separation; supersonic motion ($v_s > v$) creates a shock cone with $\sin\theta = v/v_s = 1/M$.

topics.title: Fluid Mechanics
topics.summary: Covers Chapter 14 fluid statics and fluid dynamics: density, hydrostatic pressure with depth, gauge vs. absolute pressure, barometers and manometers, Pascal's principle in hydraulics, Archimedes' principle and buoyancy, ideal fluid continuity, Bernoulli's equation and Prandtl/Pitot velocity measurement, viscosity, and Poiseuille's law for laminar pipe flow.
keyPoints: Pressure is normal force per unit area ($p = F/A$, SI unit $1\text{ Pa} = 1\text{ N/m}^2$) and acts perpendicular to any submerged surface in all directions.
In a constant-density fluid at rest, pressure decreases linearly with upward height ($dp/dy = -\rho g$) and increases linearly with depth $h$: $p = p_0 + \rho g h$, independent of container shape.

Absolute pressure equals gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure ($p_{\text{abs}} = p_{\text{g}} + p_{\text{atm}}$, with $1\text{ atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5\text{ Pa} = 760\text{ mmHg} = 1.013\text{ bar} = 14.7\text{ psi}$).
Pascal's principle states that any pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid transmits undiminished everywhere, giving hydraulic force multiplication $F_2 = (A_2/A_1)F_1$.

Archimedes' principle states that the upward buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid: $F_{\text{B}} = w_{\text{fl}} = \rho_{\text{fl}} V_{\text{sub}} g$; a floating object satisfies $F_{\text{B}} = w_{\text{obj}}$.

For incompressible steady flow, volume flow rate is constant ($Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$), so fluid speeds up in narrower sections; Bernoulli's equation ($p + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g y = \text{const}$) shows faster flow at constant height lowers static pressure.

Real viscous fluids exhibit shear drag ($F = \eta v A / L$), a parabolic velocity profile in pipes, and Poiseuille laminar flow $Q = (p_2 - p_1)\pi r^4 / (8\eta l)$, making flow rate proportional to $r^4$ and flow resistance $R = 8\eta l / (\pi r^4)$.

topics.title: Thermodynamics: First Law, Processes & Heat Engines
topics.summary: Covers thermodynamic systems (open, closed, isolated), ideal gas laws and kinetic molecular theory (average kinetic energy, rms speed, monatomic internal energy), mechanical work on p-V diagrams, the First Law of Thermodynamics (ΔE_int = Q - W), the four fundamental gas processes (isochoric, isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic), molar heat capacities (C_V, C_P, γ), heat engines, and the Carnot cycle and efficiency limit.
keyPoints: Ideal gas law: $pV = N k_{\mathrm{B}} T = nRT$, where $p$ is absolute pressure (Pa), $V$ is volume ($\mathrm{m^3}$), and $T$ MUST be absolute temperature in Kelvin ($\mathrm{K} = ^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273$).

Average translational kinetic energy per molecule is $\bar{K} = \frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T$ and rms speed is $v_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T / m}$; for an ideal monatomic gas, $E_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{3}{2} N k_{\mathrm{B}} T = \frac{3}{2} nRT$ depends solely on $T$.

First Law sign convention (SCPY130): $\Delta E_{\mathrm{int}} = Q - W$, where $Q > 0$ is heat entering the system and $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} p\,dV$ is work done BY the system ($W > 0$ for expansion, $W < 0$ for compression).
$\Delta E_{\mathrm{int}}$ is a state function (path-independent, $\Delta E_{\mathrm{int}} = 0$ over any closed cycle), whereas $W$ (signed area under the $p$-$V$ curve) and $Q$ are path-dependent.
Isochoric ($\Delta V = 0$): $W = 0$ and $\Delta U = Q = n C_V \Delta T$. Isobaric ($\Delta p = 0$): $W = p\Delta V = nR\Delta T$, $Q = n C_P \Delta T$, with Mayer's relation $C_P - C_V = R$.

Isothermal ($\Delta T = 0$, ideal gas): $\Delta U = 0$ so $Q = W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$. Adiabatic ($Q = 0$): $\Delta U = -W$, $pV^\gamma = \text{const}$, and $TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const}$ with $\gamma = C_P/C_V = 5/3 \approx 1.67$ (monatomic).

Heat engine: $W = Q_{\mathrm{h}} - Q_{\mathrm{c}}$ and efficiency $e = W/Q_{\mathrm{h}} = 1 - Q_{\mathrm{c}}/Q_{\mathrm{h}}$. By Carnot's Principle, no engine between reservoirs $T_{\mathrm{h}}$ and $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ can exceed $e_{\mathrm{Carnot}} = 1 - T_{\mathrm{c}}/T_{\mathrm{h}}$ (with $T$ in Kelvin).

formulas.name: Frequency, Period, and Angular Frequency
formulas.variables: $f$: frequency (Hz or $\text{s}^{-1}$), $T$: period (s), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Converting between oscillation period, linear frequency in Hz, and angular frequency in rad/s for any periodic motion.
formulas.pitfall: Do not plug linear frequency $f$ directly into trigonometric arguments like $\cos(ft)$ or formula denominators that require angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$.

formulas.name: Hooke's Law and SHM Equation of Motion
formulas.variables: $F_x$: restoring force (N), $k$: spring constant (N/m), $x$: displacement from equilibrium (m), $m$: mass (kg), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Identifying SHM from a force law or differential equation and extracting $\omega^2$ directly as the positive coefficient multiplying $-x$.
formulas.pitfall: Omitting the negative sign in F_x = -kx or forgetting that displacement x must be measured from the equilibrium position.

formulas.name: General Kinematics of SHM
formulas.latex: x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi), \quad v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi), \quad a(t) = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t + \phi)
formulas.variables: $x(t)$: position (m), $v(t)$: velocity (m/s), $a(t)$: acceleration ($\text{m/s}^2$), $A$: amplitude (m), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $t$: time (s), $\phi$: phase constant (rad)
formulas.whenToUse: Finding position, velocity, or acceleration at any time t given amplitude, angular frequency, and initial phase.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting to use radians on calculators when evaluating $\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ and $\sin(\omega t + \phi)$, or dropping the minus sign and factor of $\omega$ when differentiating.

formulas.name: Maximum Speed and Maximum Acceleration in SHM
formulas.variables: $|v_{\max}|$: maximum speed (m/s), $|a_{\max}|$: maximum acceleration magnitude ($\text{m/s}^2$), $A$: amplitude (m), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Quickly finding peak speed (at $x = 0$) or peak acceleration (at $x = \pm A$), or solving for $\omega = |a_{\max}|/|v_{\max}|$ and $A = |v_{\max}|^2/|a_{\max}|$.
formulas.pitfall: Confusing where each maximum occurs: speed is maximum at equilibrium ($x = 0$, where $a = 0$), whereas acceleration is maximum at the turning points ($x = \pm A$, where $v = 0$).

formulas.name: Mass-Spring Angular Frequency, Period, and Frequency
formulas.variables: $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $T$: period (s), $f$: frequency (Hz), $k$: spring force constant (N/m), $m$: oscillating mass (kg)
formulas.whenToUse: Determining the natural oscillation frequency or period of a horizontal or vertical ideal mass-spring system.
formulas.pitfall: Inverting m/k and k/m inside the square root, or assuming that changing the amplitude A changes T or f.

formulas.name: Total Mechanical Energy in SHM
formulas.variables: $E_{\text{Total}}$: total mechanical energy (J), $U$: elastic potential energy (J), $K$: kinetic energy (J), $k$: spring constant (N/m), $x$: displacement (m), $m$: mass (kg), $v$: speed (m/s), $A$: amplitude (m), $v_{\max}$: maximum speed (m/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Relating position and speed without needing time $t$ or phase $\phi$, or finding amplitude $A$ from total energy.
formulas.pitfall: Thinking total energy doubles when amplitude doubles; $E_{\text{Total}}$ scales with $A^2$, so doubling $A$ quadruples $E_{\text{Total}}$.

formulas.name: Velocity as a Function of Position in SHM
formulas.variables: $v$: velocity (m/s), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $A$: amplitude (m), $x$: displacement from equilibrium (m)
formulas.whenToUse: Calculating speed or velocity at a specific displacement $x$ when energy conservation applies, or computing $A = \sqrt{x^2 + (v/\omega)^2}$.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting that two velocities (+v and -v) are possible at every interior point |x| < A depending on the direction of motion.

formulas.name: Simple Pendulum Restoring Torque, Frequency, and Period
formulas.variables: $\tau$: restoring torque (N$\cdot$m), $L$: pendulum length (m), $m$: bob mass (kg), $g$: gravitational acceleration ($\text{m/s}^2$), $\theta$: angular displacement (rad), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $T$: period (s)
formulas.whenToUse: Small-angle oscillations (typically $\theta \lesssim 15^\circ$) of a point-like mass suspended by a light string or rod of length $L$.
formulas.pitfall: Thinking the period depends on the bob mass $m$, or forgetting that $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ requires $\theta$ in radians and breaks down at large angles.

formulas.name: Physical Pendulum Equation, Angular Frequency, and Period
formulas.variables: $I$: moment of inertia about the pivot ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$), $\alpha$: angular acceleration ($\text{rad/s}^2$), $\tau_{\text{net}}$: net torque about pivot (N$\cdot$m), $m$: mass (kg), $g$: gravitational acceleration ($\text{m/s}^2$), $L$: distance from pivot to center of mass (m), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $T$: period (s)
formulas.whenToUse: Small-angle oscillations of an extended rigid body pivoted at a distance L from its center of mass.
formulas.pitfall: Using total beam length instead of the pivot-to-CM distance $L$ (e.g., $L = \ell/2$ for a uniform rod of length $\ell$ pivoted at one end), or using $I_{\text{CM}}$ instead of $I$ about the pivot via the parallel-axis theorem.

formulas.name: Damped Oscillation Differential Equation and Solution
formulas.latex: m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + b\frac{dx}{dt} + kx = 0, \quad x(t) = A_0 e^{-\frac{b}{2m}t}\cos(\omega t + \phi)
formulas.variables: $m$: mass (kg), $b$: damping constant (kg/s or N$\cdot$s/m), $k$: spring constant (N/m), $x(t)$: displacement (m), $A_0$: initial amplitude (m), $\omega$: damped angular frequency (rad/s), $\phi$: phase constant (rad), $t$: time (s)
formulas.whenToUse: Modeling underdamped oscillators experiencing linear viscous drag F_D = -bv and finding the decaying amplitude envelope A(t) = A_0 e^{-(b/2m)t}.
formulas.pitfall: Writing e^{-(b/m)t} instead of e^{-(b/2m)t} in the amplitude decay factor (missing the factor of 2 in the denominator).

formulas.name: Damped Angular Frequency and Critical Damping Condition
formulas.variables: $\omega$: damped angular frequency (rad/s), $\omega_0$: undamped natural angular frequency (rad/s), $k$: spring constant (N/m), $m$: mass (kg), $b$: damping constant (kg/s), $b_{\text{crit}}$: critical damping constant (kg/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Finding the oscillation frequency under light damping or classifying regimes: underdamped (b^2 < 4mk), critically damped (b^2 = 4mk), and overdamped (b^2 > 4mk).
formulas.pitfall: Assuming damping increases the frequency; damping lowers $\omega$ relative to $\omega_0$ and therefore slightly lengthens the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$.

formulas.name: Forced Oscillation Differential Equation
formulas.variables: $k$: spring constant (N/m), $b$: damping constant (kg/s), $F_0$: driving force amplitude (N), $\omega$: driving angular frequency (rad/s), $m$: mass (kg), $x$: displacement (m), $t$: time (s)
formulas.whenToUse: Describing a damped spring-mass system driven by a periodic external force $F(t) = F_0\sin(\omega t)$.
formulas.pitfall: Confusing the external driving angular frequency $\omega$ with the system's undamped natural angular frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$.

formulas.name: Steady-State Amplitude in Forced Oscillations
formulas.variables: $A$: steady-state oscillation amplitude (m), $F_0$: driving force amplitude (N), $m$: mass (kg), $\omega$: driving angular frequency (rad/s), $\omega_0$: natural angular frequency $\sqrt{k/m}$ (rad/s), $b$: damping constant (kg/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Computing steady-state oscillation amplitude at any driving frequency $\omega$ and analyzing resonance peaks near $\omega \approx \omega_0$.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting to square the mass $m$ in $m^2(\omega^2 - \omega_0^2)^2$ or omitting the damping term $b^2\omega^2$ at resonance where $\omega = \omega_0$.

formulas.name: Wave Speed (Wavelength-Frequency Relation)
formulas.variables: $v$: wave speed (m/s), $\lambda$: wavelength (m), $T$: period (s), $f$: frequency (Hz)
formulas.whenToUse: Relating wave speed, wavelength, period, and frequency for any periodic traveling or standing wave.
formulas.pitfall: Confusing crest-to-trough time ($T/2$) with the full period $T$, or crest-to-trough horizontal distance ($\lambda/2$) with $\lambda$.

formulas.name: Wave Number and Angular Wave Speed
formulas.variables: $k$: wave number (rad/m), $\lambda$: wavelength (m), $\omega$: angular frequency ($\omega = 2\pi f$, rad/s), $v$: wave speed (m/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Extracting wavelength, frequency, and wave speed directly from a sinusoidal wave function $y(x, t)$.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting the $2\pi$ factor when converting between $k$ and $\lambda$ or between $\omega$ and $f$.

formulas.name: Sinusoidal Periodic Wave Equation
formulas.variables: $y$: transverse displacement (m), $A$: amplitude (m), $k$: wave number (rad/m), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $\phi$: phase constant (rad)
formulas.whenToUse: Describing wave displacement as a function of position $x$ and time $t$, or finding transverse velocity $v_y = \partial y/\partial t$.
formulas.pitfall: Sign mistake on direction: $kx - \omega t$ moves in $+x$, while $kx + \omega t$ moves in $-x$. Also, peak-to-trough height is $2A$, not $A$.

formulas.name: Linear Mass Density of a String
formulas.variables: $\mu$: linear mass density (kg/m), $m$: total string mass (kg), $L$: total string length (m)
formulas.whenToUse: Computing mass per unit length of a uniform rope or wire before calculating wave speed or wave power.
formulas.pitfall: Using total mass $m$ instead of linear density $\mu = m/L$ in $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$, or forgetting to convert g/cm to kg/m.

formulas.name: Wave Speed on a Stretched String
formulas.variables: $|v|$: wave or pulse speed (m/s), $F_T$: string tension (N), $\mu$: linear mass density (kg/m)
formulas.whenToUse: Finding mechanical wave or pulse speed on a string under tension $F_T$.
formulas.pitfall: Assuming changing amplitude or frequency changes wave speed on a string; $v$ depends solely on tension $F_T$ and linear density $\mu$.

formulas.name: Speed of a Compression Wave in a Fluid
formulas.variables: $v$: compression wave speed (m/s), $B$: bulk modulus (Pa), $\rho$: fluid mass density ($\text{kg/m}^3$)
formulas.whenToUse: Calculating sound or longitudinal compression wave speed in a liquid or gas from its bulk modulus and density.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting the square root or mixing up $\text{g/cm}^3$ with $\text{kg/m}^3$ ($\rho = 1\,\text{g/cm}^3 = 1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$).

formulas.name: Mechanical Energy in One Wavelength
formulas.variables: $E_\lambda$: total energy per wavelength (J), $U_\lambda$: potential energy (J), $K_\lambda$: kinetic energy (J), $\mu$: linear density (kg/m), $A$: amplitude (m), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $\lambda$: wavelength (m)
formulas.whenToUse: Computing kinetic, potential, or total mechanical energy contained in one full wavelength of a string wave.
formulas.pitfall: Confusing $K_\lambda = U_\lambda = \frac{1}{4}\mu A^2 \omega^2 \lambda$ with total energy $E_\lambda = \frac{1}{2}\mu A^2 \omega^2 \lambda$.

formulas.name: Average Power Transmitted by a String Wave
formulas.variables: $P_{\text{ave}}$: time-averaged power (W), $\mu$: linear mass density (kg/m), $A$: amplitude (m), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s), $v$: wave speed (m/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Calculating rate of energy transport along a taut string or comparing power scaling with amplitude and frequency.
formulas.pitfall: Omitting the $1/2$ factor, failing to square $A$ or $\omega$, or using frequency $f$ (Hz) directly instead of $\omega = 2\pi f$.

formulas.name: Wave Intensity and Spherical Inverse-Square Law
formulas.variables: $I$: wave intensity ($\text{W/m}^2$), $P$: source power (W), $A$: cross-sectional area ($\text{m}^2$), $r$: distance from point source (m)
formulas.whenToUse: Relating wave power, area, and distance for an isotropic point source radiating uniformly in 3D space.
formulas.pitfall: Using $1/r$ scaling instead of $1/r^2$ for intensity, or using circle area $\pi r^2$ instead of spherical surface area $A = 4\pi r^2$.

formulas.name: Superposition of Two Phase-Shifted Identical Waves
formulas.variables: $y_R$: resultant displacement (m), $A$: amplitude of each wave (m), $\phi$: phase difference (rad)
formulas.whenToUse: Finding the resultant waveform and amplitude when two identical traveling waves overlap with phase shift $\phi$.
formulas.pitfall: Evaluating $\cos(\phi)$ instead of $\cos(\phi/2)$ or dropping the factor of $2$ in the resultant amplitude $|2A\cos(\phi/2)|$.

formulas.name: Standing Wave Equation
formulas.variables: $y$: displacement (m), $A$: amplitude of each traveling component (m), $k$: wave number (rad/m), $\omega$: angular frequency (rad/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Analyzing nodes ($\sin(kx) = 0$), antinodes ($|\sin(kx)| = 1$), and local oscillation amplitude $|2A\sin(kx)|$ on a standing wave.
formulas.pitfall: Thinking the antinode amplitude is $A$ instead of $2A$, or assuming a standing wave transfers net energy along the string.

formulas.name: Standing Wave Normal Modes (Fixed Both Ends)
formulas.variables: $\lambda_n$: $n$-th harmonic wavelength (m), $L$: string length (m), $n$: harmonic number, $f_n$: $n$-th resonant frequency (Hz), $f_1$: fundamental frequency (Hz)
formulas.whenToUse: Finding resonant wavelengths, harmonic frequencies, and node/antinode counts on a string with symmetric fixed-end boundary conditions.
formulas.pitfall: Counting total nodes ($n+1$) as the harmonic number $n$ instead of counting the number of half-wavelength loops (antinodes).

formulas.name: Beat Frequency
formulas.variables: $f_{\text{beat}}$: beat frequency (Hz), $f_1, f_2$: frequencies of the two interfering waves (Hz)
formulas.whenToUse: Determining the loudness modulation rate when two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere.
formulas.pitfall: Dividing $|f_2 - f_1|$ by $2$ because the slow cosine envelope has frequency $|f_2 - f_1|/2$; each cycle has two loudness peaks, so $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_2 - f_1|$.

formulas.name: General Doppler Shift Equation
formulas.variables: $f_o$: observed frequency (Hz), $f_s$: source frequency (Hz), $v$: wave speed in medium (m/s), $v_o$: observer speed (m/s), $v_s$: source speed (m/s)
formulas.whenToUse: Calculating observed frequency whenever a sound source and/or observer moves relative to the medium.
formulas.pitfall: Reversing the signs: use $+v_o$ (numerator) and $-v_s$ (denominator) for motion toward each other; use $-v_o$ and $+v_s$ for motion away.

formulas.name: Mach Number and Shock Wave Cone Angle
formulas.variables: $M$: Mach number (dimensionless), $v_s$: source speed (m/s), $v$: wave speed in medium (m/s), $\theta$: Mach cone half-angle (rad or deg)
formulas.whenToUse: Analyzing supersonic sources ($v_s > v$), sonic boom geometry, and bow-wake or shock-front angles.
formulas.pitfall: Using $\tan\theta = 1/M$ instead of $\sin\theta = 1/M$, or inverting Mach number as $v/v_s$.

formulas.name: Mass Density
formulas.variables: $\rho$: density ($\text{kg/m}^3$), m: mass ($\text{kg}$), V: volume ($\text{m}^3$)
formulas.whenToUse: When relating the mass and volume of a uniform substance or fluid (e.g., fresh water $\rho = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$).
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting to convert $\text{g/cm}^3$ to $\text{kg/m}^3$ ($1\text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$) or $\text{L}$ to $\text{m}^3$ ($1\text{ L} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$).

formulas.name: Fluid Pressure
formulas.variables: p: pressure ($\text{Pa} = \text{N/m}^2$), F: normal force ($\text{N}$), A: surface area ($\text{m}^2$)
formulas.whenToUse: When computing pressure from a perpendicular force distributed over a surface, or force from uniform pressure ($F = pA$).
formulas.pitfall: Using diameter instead of radius in $A = \pi r^2$, or forgetting that hydrostatic pressure on a vertical wall varies with depth so average pressure $p_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\rho g h$ must be used.

formulas.name: Hydrostatic Pressure Differential
formulas.variables: p: fluid pressure ($\text{Pa}$), y: upward vertical coordinate ($\text{m}$), $\rho$: fluid density ($\text{kg/m}^3$), g: gravitational acceleration ($\text{m/s}^2$)
formulas.whenToUse: When analyzing how static fluid pressure varies with vertical position $y$ (especially if density varies with height, or deriving $p(h)$).
formulas.pitfall: Getting the sign backward: $y$ points upward, so pressure decreases as $y$ increases ($dp/dy < 0$) and increases going deeper ($y = -h$).

formulas.name: Pressure at Depth (Constant Density)
formulas.variables: p: absolute pressure at depth h ($\text{Pa}$), $p_0$: surface/atmospheric pressure ($\text{Pa}$), $\rho$: fluid density ($\text{kg/m}^3$), g: $9.80\text{ m/s}^2$, h: vertical depth below surface ($\text{m}$)
formulas.whenToUse: For a static, incompressible fluid of uniform density to find pressure at depth $h$, or to analyze barometers ($p_0 = 0$) and U-tube manometers.
formulas.pitfall: Using slant distance along a tilted wall or pipe instead of vertical depth $h$, or omitting $p_0$ when absolute pressure is asked.

formulas.name: Absolute and Gauge Pressure
formulas.variables: $p_{\text{abs}}$: absolute (total) pressure ($\text{Pa}$), $p_{\text{g}}$: gauge pressure relative to atmosphere ($\text{Pa}$), $p_{\text{atm}}$: atmospheric pressure ($1.013 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$)
formulas.whenToUse: Whenever converting between gauge readings (e.g., tire or tank gauges, $\rho g h$ fluid column) and total absolute pressure.
formulas.pitfall: Adding $p_{\text{atm}}$ twice or subtracting $p_{\text{atm}}$ when finding $p_{\text{abs}}$ from $p_{\text{g}}$.

formulas.name: Pascal's Principle (Hydraulic Systems)
formulas.variables: $F_1, F_2$: forces on input and output pistons ($\text{N}$), $A_1, A_2$: piston cross-sectional areas ($\text{m}^2$)
formulas.whenToUse: For enclosed hydraulic lifts, presses, or brake cylinders whose pistons are at the same elevation ($\Delta p_1 = \Delta p_2$).
formulas.pitfall: Scaling force by the radius ratio $r_2/r_1$ instead of the area ratio $(r_2/r_1)^2 = (d_2/d_1)^2$, or assuming energy is multiplied (work $F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2$ is conserved).

formulas.name: Archimedes' Principle (Buoyant Force)
formulas.variables: $F_{\text{B}}$: upward buoyant force ($\text{N}$), $w_{\text{fl}}$: weight of displaced fluid ($\text{N}$), $\rho_{\text{fl}}$: fluid density ($\text{kg/m}^3$), $V_{\text{sub}}$: submerged volume of object ($\text{m}^3$), g: $9.80\text{ m/s}^2$
formulas.whenToUse: For any object wholly or partially submerged in a fluid, to calculate apparent weight ($T = w_{\text{obj}} - F_{\text{B}}$) or floating submerged fraction ($V_{\text{sub}}/V_{\text{obj}} = \rho_{\text{obj}}/\rho_{\text{fl}}$).
formulas.pitfall: Using the object's density $\rho_{\text{obj}}$ instead of the fluid's density $\rho_{\text{fl}}$ in $F_{\text{B}}$, or using total object volume instead of submerged volume $V_{\text{sub}}$ for floating bodies.

formulas.name: Volume Flow Rate
formulas.variables: Q: volume flow rate ($\text{m}^3/\text{s}$), V: fluid volume ($\text{m}^3$), t: time ($\text{s}$), A: cross-sectional area ($\text{m}^2$), v: fluid speed ($\text{m/s}$)
formulas.whenToUse: To convert between flow rate (often given in $\text{L/s}$) and average fluid velocity in a pipe of area $A$.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting $1\text{ L/s} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$, or plugging diameter into $A = \pi r^2$ without halving it.

formulas.name: Equation of Continuity (Incompressible)
formulas.variables: $A_1, A_2$: cross-sectional areas at points 1 and 2 ($\text{m}^2$), $v_1, v_2$: fluid speeds at points 1 and 2 ($\text{m/s}$)
formulas.whenToUse: For steady, incompressible (constant-density) fluid flow through a pipe or stream tube of changing cross-sectional area.
formulas.pitfall: Assuming speed scales inversely with radius $r$ instead of $r^2$ ($v_2 = v_1(r_1/r_2)^2$), or failing to sum parallel branch areas when a pipe splits.

formulas.name: Continuity Equation (General Form)
formulas.variables: $\rho_1, \rho_2$: fluid densities ($\text{kg/m}^3$), $A_1, A_2$: cross-sectional areas ($\text{m}^2$), $v_1, v_2$: fluid speeds ($\text{m/s}$)
formulas.whenToUse: When fluid density can vary between two cross sections (compressible gas flow), expressing conservation of mass flow rate $\dot{m} = \rho A v$.
formulas.pitfall: Applying simplified $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ to a compressible gas undergoing strong pressure/density changes.

formulas.name: Bernoulli's Equation
formulas.latex: p_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g y_1 = p_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g y_2
formulas.variables: p: static pressure ($\text{Pa}$), $\rho$: fluid density ($\text{kg/m}^3$), v: fluid speed ($\text{m/s}$), g: $9.80\text{ m/s}^2$, y: vertical elevation ($\text{m}$)
formulas.whenToUse: Along a streamline for steady, incompressible, frictionless (nonviscous) flow to relate pressure, speed, and height (including Venturi meters and Prandtl/Pitot tubes where $v_1 = 0$).
formulas.pitfall: Using Bernoulli's equation when significant viscosity/turbulence is present, mixing gauge and absolute pressures on opposite sides, or reversing the sign of $\frac{1}{2}\rho(v_1^2 - v_2^2)$.

formulas.name: Viscous Shear Force
formulas.variables: F: tangential force to maintain relative plate speed ($\text{N}$), $\eta$: coefficient of viscosity ($\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}$), v: relative speed ($\text{m/s}$), A: plate surface area ($\text{m}^2$), L: fluid layer thickness ($\text{m}$)
formulas.whenToUse: When calculating the viscous drag force required to move a flat plate of area $A$ at steady speed $v$ across a thin fluid film of thickness $L$.
formulas.pitfall: Missing the $10^{-3}$ factor commonly placed in viscosity table headers ($\eta \times 10^{-3}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$) or confusing film thickness $L$ with plate area $A$.

formulas.name: Poiseuille's Law
formulas.variables: Q: laminar volume flow rate ($\text{m}^3/\text{s}$), $p_2 - p_1$: driving pressure drop ($\text{Pa}$), r: pipe inner radius ($\text{m}$), $\eta$: viscosity ($\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}$), l: pipe length ($\text{m}$)
formulas.whenToUse: For steady laminar flow of a viscous, incompressible fluid through a uniform cylindrical tube or blood vessel.
formulas.pitfall: Using diameter instead of radius in $r^4$ (which introduces a factor of $2^4 = 16$ error!) or raising $r$ to the 2nd power instead of the 4th power.

formulas.name: Poiseuille's Law for Resistance
formulas.variables: R: fluid flow resistance ($\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s/m}^3$), $\eta$: viscosity ($\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}$), l: tube length ($\text{m}$), r: tube inner radius ($\text{m}$)
formulas.whenToUse: When comparing how tube geometry or viscosity resists flow via $Q = (p_2 - p_1)/R$, especially when vessel radius narrows.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting that halving the radius increases resistance by $2^4 = 16\times$ and reduces flow rate to $1/16$ at constant pressure drop.

formulas.name: Ideal Gas Law (Molecular Form)
formulas.variables: p: absolute pressure (Pa), V: volume (m^3), N: number of molecules (dimensionless), k_B: Boltzmann constant (1.38e-23 J/K), T: absolute temperature (K)
formulas.whenToUse: Use when counting individual gas molecules N or working directly with molecular kinetic energy via k_B.
formulas.pitfall: Never plug Celsius into T or gauge pressure into p; convert °C to K (T = t + 273) and liters to m^3 (1 L = 10^-3 m^3).

formulas.name: Ideal Gas Law (Molar Form) & Combined Gas Law
formulas.variables: p: absolute pressure (Pa), V: volume (m^3), n: number of moles (mol), R: universal gas constant = N_A k_B = 8.31 J/(mol·K), T: absolute temperature (K)
formulas.whenToUse: Use pV = nRT when moles n are given, or p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2 when comparing two equilibrium states of a fixed amount of gas.
formulas.pitfall: In the ratio p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2, p and V units just need to match on both sides, but T MUST still be in Kelvin—never °C.

formulas.name: Average Molecular Kinetic Energy & RMS Speed
formulas.latex: \bar{K} = \frac{1}{2} m \overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T, \qquad v_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{m}}
formulas.variables: K_bar: average translational kinetic energy per molecule (J), m: mass of one molecule (kg), v_rms: root-mean-square speed (m/s), k_B: 1.38e-23 J/K, T: absolute temperature (K)
formulas.whenToUse: Use to find mean translational kinetic energy from temperature alone, or rms molecular speed from temperature and single-molecule mass m.
formulas.pitfall: Remember m is the mass of ONE molecule in kg (not molar mass in g/mol). Also, doubling v_rms requires quadrupling absolute temperature T.

formulas.name: Internal Energy of an Ideal Monatomic Gas
formulas.latex: E_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{3}{2} N k_{\mathrm{B}} T = \frac{3}{2} n R T
formulas.variables: E_int: internal energy (J), N: number of molecules, n: moles (mol), k_B: 1.38e-23 J/K, R: 8.31 J/(mol·K), T: absolute temperature (K)
formulas.whenToUse: Use to find the internal energy (or ΔE_int = 3/2 nR ΔT) of a monatomic ideal gas such as He or Ar at temperature T.
formulas.pitfall: The 3/2 factor applies strictly to monatomic ideal gases (3 translational degrees of freedom); for general ideal gases, use ΔU = n C_V ΔT.

formulas.name: Work Done by a Thermodynamic System
formulas.variables: W: work done BY the system (J), p: pressure (Pa), V: volume (m^3), V_1/V_2: initial/final volumes (m^3)
formulas.whenToUse: Use to compute work as the signed area under a p-V process curve between V_1 and V_2.
formulas.pitfall: Work is path-dependent and positive only during expansion (V_2 > V_1); during compression (V_2 < V_1), W < 0. Watch unit conversion: 1 L·atm ≈ 101 J.

formulas.name: First Law of Thermodynamics
formulas.variables: ΔE_int (or ΔU): change in internal energy (J), Q: net heat added to system (J), W: work done BY system (J)
formulas.whenToUse: Applies to EVERY thermodynamic process between equilibrium states, including closed cycles (where ΔE_int = 0 so Q_net = W_net).
formulas.pitfall: Watch the minus sign before W! If work is done ON the system (compression), W is negative, so -W adds energy to E_int.

formulas.name: Isochoric Process & Constant-Volume Heat Capacity
formulas.latex: W = 0, \qquad \Delta U = Q = n C_V \Delta T \quad \left(C_V = \frac{3}{2} R\text{ for monatomic}\right)
formulas.variables: W: work (J), ΔU: internal energy change (J), Q: heat transferred (J), n: moles (mol), C_V: molar heat capacity at constant volume (J/(mol·K)), ΔT: temperature change (K)
formulas.whenToUse: Use when volume is constant (vertical line on p-V diagram). Also remember ΔU = n C_V ΔT holds for ANY ideal-gas process.
formulas.pitfall: Do not apply Q = n C_V ΔT when pressure or volume changes—only ΔU = n C_V ΔT is universally valid for ideal gases.

formulas.name: Isobaric Process Work & Heat
formulas.latex: W = p \Delta V = n R \Delta T, \qquad Q = n C_P \Delta T
formulas.variables: W: work done by gas (J), p: constant pressure (Pa), ΔV: V_f - V_i (m^3), n: moles (mol), R: 8.31 J/(mol·K), C_P: molar heat capacity at constant pressure (J/(mol·K)), ΔT: T_f - T_i (K)
formulas.whenToUse: Use for horizontal paths on a p-V diagram where pressure remains constant.
formulas.pitfall: Forgetting to convert ΔV from liters to m^3 (1 L = 10^-3 m^3) or using C_V instead of C_P when calculating heat Q in an isobaric process.

formulas.name: Mayer's Relation Between C_P and C_V
formulas.latex: C_P - C_V = R \quad \left(C_P = \frac{5}{2} R\text{ for monatomic}\right)
formulas.variables: C_P: molar heat capacity at constant pressure (J/(mol·K)), C_V: molar heat capacity at constant volume (J/(mol·K)), R: universal gas constant (8.31 J/(mol·K))
formulas.whenToUse: Use to find C_P from C_V (or vice versa) for any ideal gas.
formulas.pitfall: Mixing up C_P and C_V: C_P is always larger than C_V by R because extra heat is needed to do expansion work at constant pressure.

formulas.name: Isothermal Process (Ideal Gas)
formulas.latex: \Delta U = 0, \qquad Q = W = n R T \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)
formulas.variables: ΔU: internal energy change (J), Q: heat added (J), W: work done by gas (J), n: moles (mol), R: 8.31 J/(mol·K), T: constant temperature (K), V_1/V_2: initial/final volume (m^3)
formulas.whenToUse: Use when an ideal gas expands or compresses slowly at constant temperature (along a pV = const hyperbola).
formulas.pitfall: Remember ΔU = 0 does NOT mean Q = 0! Also keep the ratio as V_2/V_1 (final over initial), not V_1/V_2.

formulas.name: Adiabatic Process Equations
formulas.latex: Q = 0, \quad \Delta U = -W, \quad p_i V_i^{\gamma} = p_f V_f^{\gamma}, \quad T_i V_i^{\gamma - 1} = T_f V_f^{\gamma - 1}
formulas.variables: Q: heat transfer (0 J), ΔU: internal energy change (J), W: work done by gas (J), p: pressure (Pa), V: volume (m^3), T: absolute temperature (K), γ: C_P/C_V (dimensionless)
formulas.whenToUse: Use when a gas is thermally insulated or changes volume so rapidly that no heat flows (Q = 0).
formulas.pitfall: Using Boyle's law (p_i V_i = p_f V_f) instead of p_i V_i^γ = p_f V_f^γ, or using exponent γ instead of (γ - 1) in the T-V equation.

formulas.name: Heat Capacity Ratio (Adiabatic Index)
formulas.variables: γ: adiabatic index (dimensionless), C_P: molar heat capacity at constant pressure (J/(mol·K)), C_V: molar heat capacity at constant volume (J/(mol·K))
formulas.whenToUse: Use to compute the adiabatic exponent γ from C_P and C_V (or 5/3 for monatomic gases like He, Ne, Ar).
formulas.pitfall: Inverting the ratio to C_V/C_P; because C_P > C_V, γ is always strictly greater than 1.

formulas.name: Heat Engine Work & Thermal Efficiency
formulas.variables: W: net work output per cycle (J), Q_h: heat absorbed from hot reservoir (J), Q_c: magnitude of heat rejected to cold reservoir (J), e: thermal efficiency (dimensionless, 0 to 1)
formulas.whenToUse: Use for ANY cyclic heat engine operating between hot and cold thermal reservoirs.
formulas.pitfall: Dividing work by Q_c instead of Q_h, or confusing Q_c/Q_h with efficiency instead of 1 - Q_c/Q_h.

formulas.name: Carnot Engine Maximum Efficiency
formulas.variables: e_Carnot: maximum possible efficiency (dimensionless), T_c: cold reservoir temperature (K), T_h: hot reservoir temperature (K)
formulas.whenToUse: Use for an ideal reversible (Carnot) engine or to find the theoretical upper bound on efficiency for any engine between T_c and T_h.
formulas.pitfall: Plugging °C instead of Kelvin into T_c and T_h is the #1 exam mistake; also remember real irreversible engines always satisfy e ≤ e_Carnot.

flashcards.front: What is the defining condition of Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)?
flashcards.back: The acceleration $a_x$, and therefore the net restoring force $F_x$, is directly proportional to the displacement $x$ from equilibrium and acts in the opposite direction: $F_x = -kx$ and $a_x = -\omega^2 x$.
flashcards.hint: Opposite direction + linear proportionality to $x$.

flashcards.front: How are period $T$, frequency $f$, and angular frequency $\omega$ related, and what is $1\text{ Hz}$?
flashcards.back: $f = 1/T$ and $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi / T$. One hertz is one complete cycle per second: $1\text{ Hz} = 1\text{ cycle/s} = 1\text{ s}^{-1}$.
flashcards.hint: One full cycle spans $2\pi$ radians in time $T$.

flashcards.front: In SHM, where do $|v|$ and $|a|$ reach their maximum values and where are they zero?
flashcards.back: At equilibrium ($x = 0$): $|v| = v_{\max} = A\omega$ and $a = 0$. At the turning points ($x = \pm A$): $v = 0$ and $|a| = a_{\max} = A\omega^2$.
flashcards.hint: Speed peaks at the center; restoring force peaks at the ends.

flashcards.front: What are the phase relationships among $x(t)$, $v(t)$, and $a(t)$ in SHM?
flashcards.back: Velocity $v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi)$ leads position $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ by $\pi/2$ rad ($90^\circ$), while acceleration $a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t)$ is $\pi$ rad ($180^\circ$) out of phase with $x(t)$.
flashcards.hint: When $x$ is at $+A$, $a$ is at $-a_{\max}$ and $v = 0$.

flashcards.front: Does the period $T$ of an ideal mass-spring system or small-angle simple pendulum depend on amplitude $A$?
flashcards.back: No. In ideal SHM, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ for a mass-spring system and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ for a simple pendulum—neither depends on amplitude (nor does the pendulum period depend on bob mass $m$).
flashcards.hint: Isochronism of SHM.

flashcards.front: How does total mechanical energy $E_{\text{Total}}$ in SHM depend on amplitude $A$, and how do $U(x)$ and $K(x)$ vary with $x$?
flashcards.back: $E_{\text{Total}} = U + K = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$, so doubling $A$ quadruples $E_{\text{Total}}$. Graphically, $U(x)$ is an upward parabola and $K(x) = E_{\text{Total}} - U(x)$ is an inverted parabola meeting $0$ at $x = \pm A$.
flashcards.hint: Quadratic in both $x$ and $A$.

flashcards.front: At what displacement $x$ from equilibrium are kinetic energy $K$ and elastic potential energy $U$ equal in SHM?
flashcards.back: $x = \pm\frac{A}{\sqrt{2}} \approx \pm 0.707A$, because $U = \frac{1}{2}E_{\text{Total}} \implies \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{4}kA^2$.
flashcards.hint: Split $\frac{1}{2}kA^2$ evenly between $U$ and $K$.

flashcards.front: What approximation reduces a simple pendulum's torque equation $\tau = -Lmg\sin\theta$ to SHM?
flashcards.back: The small-angle approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ (with $\theta$ in radians), yielding $\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -\frac{g}{L}\theta$ and $\omega = \sqrt{g/L}$.
flashcards.hint: Valid for small angles in radians.

flashcards.front: In the physical pendulum formula $\omega = \sqrt{mgL/I}$, what do $L$ and $I$ represent?
flashcards.back: $L$ is the distance from the pivot point $O$ to the center of mass ($\text{CM}$), and $I$ is the rigid body's moment of inertia about the pivot $O$ (not about $\text{CM}$ unless the pivot is at $\text{CM}$). For a uniform beam of total length $\ell$ pivoted at one end, $L = \ell/2$ and $I = \frac{1}{3}m\ell^2$.
flashcards.hint: Use pivot-to-CM distance and parallel-axis theorem.

flashcards.front: How does the amplitude of a lightly damped oscillator decay over time when $F_D = -bv$?
flashcards.back: It decays exponentially inside the envelope $\pm A_0 e^{-\frac{b}{2m}t}$, according to $x(t) = A_0 e^{-\frac{b}{2m}t}\cos(\omega t + \phi)$.
flashcards.hint: Remember the $2m$ in the exponent denominator.

flashcards.front: How does light damping affect the oscillation angular frequency $\omega$ compared to the undamped natural frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$?
flashcards.back: Damping reduces the angular frequency to $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m} - \left(\frac{b}{2m}\right)^2} < \omega_0$, which slightly increases the oscillation period $T$.
flashcards.hint: The damping term subtracts inside the square root.

flashcards.front: What are the three damping regimes in terms of $b^2$ and $4mk$, and which returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating?
flashcards.back: Underdamped ($b^2 < 4mk$): oscillates with decaying amplitude. Critically damped ($b^2 = 4mk$): returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating. Overdamped ($b^2 > 4mk$): returns slowly without oscillating.
flashcards.hint: Look at the discriminant $b^2 - 4mk$ (or sign inside $\sqrt{k/m - (b/2m)^2}$).

flashcards.front: In forced oscillations, when does resonance occur and how does damping $b$ shape the amplitude vs. driving frequency curve?
flashcards.back: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches (or is near) the natural frequency ($\omega \approx \omega_0$, $f \approx f_0$), maximizing amplitude $A = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{m^2(\omega^2 - \omega_0^2)^2 + b^2\omega^2}}$. Smaller damping gives a taller, sharper peak; heavy damping lowers and flattens the peak.
flashcards.hint: Smaller $b$ means sharper, taller peak at $f_0$.

flashcards.front: How does particle oscillation direction differ between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave?
flashcards.back: In a transverse wave, medium particles oscillate perpendicular to the wave propagation velocity $\vec{v}$. In a longitudinal wave, particles oscillate parallel (back and forth) to $\vec{v}$, forming compressions and rarefactions.
flashcards.hint: Trans- means across; longi- means along.

flashcards.front: In the sinusoidal wave equation $y(x, t) = A\sin(kx \mp \omega t + \phi)$, how do you determine the propagation direction?
flashcards.back: Keep phase $kx \mp \omega t + \phi$ constant: $(kx - \omega t)$ gives $dx/dt = +\omega/k > 0$ ($+x$-direction), while $(kx + \omega t)$ gives $dx/dt = -\omega/k < 0$ ($-x$-direction).
flashcards.hint: Same sign between $kx$ and $\omega t$ travels left ($-x$); opposite signs travel right ($+x$).

flashcards.front: Distinguish wave propagation speed $v$ from the maximum transverse speed $v_{y,\max}$ of a string particle.
flashcards.back: Wave speed is $v = \omega/k = \lambda f$ (constant, set by tension and $\mu$). Transverse particle velocity is $v_y = \partial y/\partial t$, with maximum $v_{y,\max} = A\omega$ as the particle passes equilibrium ($y = 0$).
flashcards.hint: Differentiate $y(x, t)$ with respect to $t$ while holding $x$ fixed.

flashcards.front: If a wave enters a heavier rope with $4\times$ the linear mass density ($\mu_2 = 4\mu_1$) at the same tension $F_T$, how do $v$, $f$, and $\lambda$ change?
flashcards.back: Wave speed halves ($v_2 = \sqrt{F_T/(4\mu_1)} = v_1/2$), frequency stays unchanged ($f_2 = f_1$) because the boundary oscillates at the incoming rate, and wavelength halves ($\lambda_2 = v_2/f_2 = \lambda_1/2$).
flashcards.hint: Medium sets $v$; source sets $f$; $\lambda = v/f$ adjusts.

flashcards.front: What physical properties determine the speed of a longitudinal compression wave in a fluid ($v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$)?
flashcards.back: The fluid's stiffness against compression (bulk modulus $B$, in Pa) and its inertia (mass density $\rho$, in $\text{kg/m}^3$). Stiffer fluids (larger $B$) transmit waves faster; denser fluids (larger $\rho$) slow them down.
flashcards.hint: Same structural form as a string: $\sqrt{\text{elasticity}/\text{inertia}}$.

flashcards.front: How is total mechanical energy $E_\lambda$ distributed between kinetic energy $K_\lambda$ and potential energy $U_\lambda$ in one wavelength of a sinusoidal string wave?
flashcards.back: Equally: $K_\lambda = U_\lambda = \frac{1}{4}\mu A^2 \omega^2 \lambda$, so total energy per wavelength is $E_\lambda = K_\lambda + U_\lambda = \frac{1}{2}\mu A^2 \omega^2 \lambda$.
flashcards.hint: The average of $\cos^2(kx)$ and $\sin^2(kx)$ over one full wavelength is each $1/2$.

flashcards.front: In $P_{\text{ave}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu A^2 \omega^2 v$, how does average wave power scale when you double amplitude $A$ or double frequency $f$?
flashcards.back: Power scales as $A^2$ and as $\omega^2 \propto f^2$. Doubling $A$ quadruples $P_{\text{ave}}$ ($4\times$); doubling $f$ also quadruples $P_{\text{ave}}$ ($4\times$); doubling both increases power by $16\times$.
flashcards.hint: Both $A$ and $\omega$ appear squared in $P_{\text{ave}}$.

flashcards.front: For a spherical wave from a point source ($I = P/(4\pi r^2)$), how do intensity $I$ and wave amplitude $A$ vary if distance $r$ triples?
flashcards.back: Intensity drops by a factor of $3^2=9$ ($I \propto 1/r^2$). Since intensity is proportional to $A^2$, amplitude drops by a factor of $3$ ($A \propto 1/r$).
flashcards.hint: Area of a sphere grows as $r^2$, and energy/intensity scales as $A^2$.

flashcards.front: Using $y_R(x, t) = [2A\cos(\phi/2)]\sin(kx - \omega t + \phi/2)$, what resultant amplitude arises for $\phi = 0$, $\phi = \pi/2$, and $\phi = \pi$?
flashcards.back: For $\phi = 0$: $A_R = 2A\cos(0) = 2A$ (purely constructive); for $\phi = \pi/2$: $A_R = 2A\cos(\pi/4) = \sqrt{2}A$; for $\phi = \pi$: $A_R = 2A\cos(\pi/2) = 0$ (purely destructive).
flashcards.hint: Always halve $\phi$ before taking $\cos(\phi/2)$.

flashcards.front: For the standing wave $y(x, t) = [2A\sin(kx)]\cos(\omega t)$, where are nodes and antinodes located, and what is the spacing between adjacent nodes?
flashcards.back: Nodes occur where $\sin(kx) = 0$ ($x = m\lambda/2$, zero displacement at all times). Antinodes occur halfway between nodes ($x = (m + 1/2)\lambda/2$, max amplitude $2A$). Adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart.
flashcards.hint: Two adjacent nodes bracket half a wavelength, not a full wavelength.

flashcards.front: On a string of length $L$ fixed at both ends (symmetric boundary conditions), how many nodes and antinodes appear in the $n$-th harmonic?
flashcards.back: The $n$-th harmonic ($\lambda_n = 2L/n$, $f_n = nf_1$) has $n$ antinodes (half-wavelength loops) and $n + 1$ nodes (including both fixed endpoints).
flashcards.hint: $n = 1$ (fundamental) has $1$ loop and $2$ endpoint nodes.

flashcards.front: In the beat equation $y(t) = 2A\cos(2\pi f_{\text{avg}} t)\cos\left(2\pi\frac{|f_2-f_1|}{2}t\right)$, why is $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_2 - f_1|$ rather than $|f_2 - f_1|/2$?
flashcards.back: Loudness depends on the magnitude of the slow envelope $|\cos(2\pi \frac{|f_2-f_1|}{2}t)|$, which reaches maximum amplitude $2A$ at both $+1$ and $-1$ (twice per envelope cycle), so the beat rate is $f_{\text{beat}} = 2 \times \frac{|f_2-f_1|}{2} = |f_2 - f_1|$.
flashcards.hint: Both $+2A$ and $-2A$ are constructive interference peaks.

flashcards.front: Why does a moving source shift observed frequency through a different mechanism than a moving observer?
flashcards.back: A moving source physically compresses or stretches the wavelength $\lambda_O$ in the medium ($v \mp v_s$ in the denominator). A moving observer encounters unmodified wavefronts at a faster or slower relative rate ($v \pm v_o$ in the numerator).
flashcards.hint: Numerator = observer motion; denominator = source motion.

flashcards.front: How do you solve a Doppler echo problem (e.g., a bat emitting sound that reflects off a moving insect)?
flashcards.back: Apply the Doppler formula in two steps: (1) find $f_{\text{reflector}}$ heard by the insect (bat = source, insect = observer), then (2) find $f_{\text{echo}}$ heard back by the bat (insect = moving source emitting $f_{\text{reflector}}$, bat = observer).
flashcards.hint: The moving target acts first as an observer, then as a re-emitting source.

flashcards.front: What happens when a source moves faster than the wave speed in a medium ($M = v_s/v > 1$), and what is Cerenkov radiation?
flashcards.back: Successive spherical wavefronts pile up constructively along a conical shock front of half-angle $\sin\theta = v/v_s = 1/M$. Cerenkov radiation is the optical analog: subatomic particles moving faster than the speed of light in water emit a blue shock-wave glow.
flashcards.hint: Higher Mach number $M$ produces a smaller, narrower cone angle $\theta$.

flashcards.front: What is the SI unit of pressure, and what are the equivalent values of $1\text{ atm}$ in $\text{Pa}$, $\text{mmHg}$, $\text{bar}$, and $\text{psi}$?
flashcards.back: The SI unit is the pascal: $1\text{ Pa} = 1\text{ N/m}^2$. Standard atmosphere: $1\text{ atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5\text{ Pa} = 760\text{ mmHg} = 1.013\text{ bar} = 14.7\text{ psi}$ (and $1\text{ torr} = 1\text{ mmHg} = 133.3\text{ Pa}$, $1\text{ bar} = 10^5\text{ Pa}$).
flashcards.hint: Think of $760\text{ mmHg}$ and $1.013 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$.

flashcards.front: How are absolute pressure $p_{\text{abs}}$, gauge pressure $p_{\text{g}}$, and atmospheric pressure $p_{\text{atm}}$ related?
flashcards.back: $p_{\text{abs}} = p_{\text{g}} + p_{\text{atm}}$. Gauge pressure measures how much the fluid pressure exceeds (or falls below, if negative) local atmospheric pressure.
flashcards.hint: Gauge pressure is measured relative to the surrounding air.

flashcards.front: Why does $p = p_0 + \rho g h$ depend only on depth $h$ and fluid density $\rho$, not on the shape or width of the container?
flashcards.back: Because hydrostatic equilibrium gives $\frac{dp}{dy} = -\rho g$ everywhere along the vertical direction, and fluid at rest cannot sustain shear forces; all points at the same depth in a connected, uniform fluid have equal pressure.
flashcards.hint: Integrating $dp/dy = -\rho g$ depends only on vertical coordinate $y$.

flashcards.front: How does a mercury barometer measure atmospheric pressure $p_{\text{atm}}$, and how does an open U-tube with two immiscible fluids compare their densities?
flashcards.back: In a barometer, the closed top holds a vacuum ($p_{\text{top}} = 0$), so $p_{\text{atm}} = \rho_{\text{Hg}} g h$. In an open U-tube at equilibrium at the lowest interface, $p_{\text{atm}} + \rho_1 g h_1 = p_{\text{atm}} + \rho_2 g h_2 \implies \rho_1 h_1 = \rho_2 h_2$ (the less dense fluid stands taller).
flashcards.hint: Equal pressure at the same horizontal level in a continuous static fluid.

flashcards.front: State Pascal's principle and write the force-multiplication relation for a hydraulic lift.
flashcards.back: A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to all parts of the fluid and container walls: $\Delta p = \frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$, so $F_2 = \frac{A_2}{A_1} F_1$ (while work $F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2$ remains conserved).
flashcards.hint: Pressure change $\Delta p$ is uniform everywhere in the enclosed fluid.

flashcards.front: State Archimedes' principle and explain why a loaded cargo ship floats lower in the water than an unloaded ship.
flashcards.back: The upward buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid: $F_{\text{B}} = w_{\text{fl}} = \rho_{\text{fl}} V_{\text{sub}} g$. A loaded ship weighs more, so it must sink deeper to displace a larger water volume $V_{\text{sub}}$ until $F_{\text{B}} = w_{\text{ship}}$.
flashcards.hint: Equilibrium while floating requires $F_{\text{B}}$ to balance total ship weight.

flashcards.front: For a homogeneous object of density $\rho_{\text{obj}}$ floating in a liquid of density $\rho_{\text{fl}}$, what fraction of its volume is submerged?
flashcards.back: Setting $F_{\text{B}} = w_{\text{obj}}$ gives $\rho_{\text{fl}} V_{\text{sub}} g = \rho_{\text{obj}} V_{\text{obj}} g$, so the submerged fraction is $\frac{V_{\text{sub}}}{V_{\text{obj}}} = \frac{\rho_{\text{obj}}}{\rho_{\text{fl}}}$.
flashcards.hint: Balance buoyant force against object weight.

flashcards.front: Contrast an ideal fluid, laminar flow, and turbulent flow.
flashcards.back: An ideal fluid has negligible viscosity (and is incompressible). In laminar flow, adjacent fluid layers slide smoothly in parallel paths without mixing. In turbulent flow, irregular eddies and swirls mix layers, causing greater heating and higher flow resistance.
flashcards.hint: Smooth parallel layers vs. mixing eddies and swirls.

flashcards.front: What conservation laws yield the Continuity Equation ($A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$) and Bernoulli's Equation ($p + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g y = \text{const}$)?
flashcards.back: Continuity comes from conservation of mass (for constant density, constant volume flow rate $Q = Av$). Bernoulli's equation comes from conservation of energy (work-energy theorem) for steady, incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline.
flashcards.hint: One is mass conservation; the other is work-energy per unit volume.

flashcards.front: How does a Prandtl (Pitot) tube use Bernoulli's equation to measure fluid speed $v_2$?
flashcards.back: Tube 1 faces the oncoming flow, creating a stagnation dead spot ($v_1 = 0$), while Tube 2 has a side opening where the fluid flows past at $v_2$ at the same height. Bernoulli gives $p_1 - p_2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$, so the manometer height difference $h \propto \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$.
flashcards.hint: Compare static pressure at the side port with stagnation pressure at the nose ($v_1 = 0$).

flashcards.front: How does the velocity profile in a circular pipe differ between a nonviscous fluid ($\eta = 0$) and a viscous fluid ($\eta > 0$)?
flashcards.back: A nonviscous fluid moves with a uniform speed across the entire cross section, whereas a viscous fluid has a parabolic velocity profile: speed is slowest (zero) at the pipe walls due to friction and fastest at the center.
flashcards.hint: Wall drag slows down the outer layers.

flashcards.front: According to the EP9 viscosity tables, how does temperature affect the viscosity $\eta$ of liquids (like blood) versus gases (like air)?
flashcards.back: In liquids, viscosity decreases as temperature rises (e.g., whole blood drops from $3.015 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$ to $2.084 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$ at $37^\circ\text{C}$). In gases like air, viscosity increases slightly as temperature rises ($0.0171$ to $0.0218 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$ from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $100^\circ\text{C}$).
flashcards.hint: Hot syrup flows faster, while hotter gas molecules transfer momentum faster.

flashcards.front: Under Poiseuille's law, if a circular tube's radius $r$ is halved while pressure drop $p_2 - p_1$, length $l$, and viscosity $\eta$ stay constant, how do flow rate $Q$ and resistance $R$ change?
flashcards.back: Because $Q = \frac{(p_2 - p_1)\pi r^4}{8\eta l}$ and $R = \frac{8\eta l}{\pi r^4}$, halving $r$ increases resistance $R$ by $2^4 = 16\times$ and reduces flow rate $Q$ to $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$ of its original value.
flashcards.hint: Remember the fourth-power sensitivity $r^4$!

flashcards.front: In SCPY130 thermodynamics, how do an **isolated/closed system** and an **open system** differ?
flashcards.back: An **isolated/closed system** is completely separated from its surroundings (immovable, thermally insulating walls; no exchange), whereas an **open system** (e.g., a boiling tea kettle) exchanges energy and/or matter with its surroundings across its boundary.
flashcards.hint: Think boiling kettle vs. sealed insulated container.

flashcards.front: What are the two forms of the ideal gas law and the numerical values of $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $R$?
flashcards.back: $pV = N k_{\mathrm{B}} T$ with $k_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J/K}$, and $pV = nRT$ with $R = N_{\mathrm{A}} k_{\mathrm{B}} = 8.31\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$. $T$ must be in Kelvin.
flashcards.hint: One uses molecule count $N$; the other uses moles $n$.

flashcards.front: What determines the average translational kinetic energy $\bar{K}$ and rms speed $v_{\mathrm{rms}}$ of ideal gas molecules?
flashcards.back: $\bar{K} = \frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T$ depends ONLY on absolute temperature $T$, while $v_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{m}}$ also depends inversely on $\sqrt{m}$ (lighter molecules move faster at the same $T$).
flashcards.hint: Same $T$ means same $\bar{K}$, not same speed.

flashcards.front: What is the internal energy $E_{\mathrm{int}}$ of $n$ moles of an ideal monatomic gas?
flashcards.back: $E_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{3}{2} N k_{\mathrm{B}} T = \frac{3}{2} nRT$. Because $E_{\mathrm{int}}$ depends only on temperature $T$, $\Delta E_{\mathrm{int}}$ is path-independent.
flashcards.hint: Multiply $\bar{K} = \frac{3}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ by $N$ molecules.

flashcards.front: State the First Law of Thermodynamics and the sign conventions for $Q$ and $W$ used in SCPY130.
flashcards.back: $\Delta E_{\mathrm{int}} = Q - W$, where $Q > 0$ means heat enters the system ($Q < 0$ leaves) and $W = \int p\,dV > 0$ means work is done BY the system during expansion ($W < 0$ on compression).
flashcards.hint: Heat IN minus work BY equals change in internal energy.

flashcards.front: Why do different paths between states $A$ and $B$ on a $p$-$V$ diagram have the same $\Delta E_{\mathrm{int}}$ but different $W$ and $Q$?
flashcards.back: $E_{\mathrm{int}}$ is a state function depending only on the endpoints ($T_A, T_B$), so $\Delta E_{\mathrm{int}}$ is path-independent. $W = \int p\,dV$ is the area under the specific $p$-$V$ curve, so both $W$ and $Q = \Delta E_{\mathrm{int}} + W$ depend on the path.
flashcards.hint: Compare endpoint coordinates vs. area under the curve.

flashcards.front: Summarize an **isochoric process** ($V = \text{const}$) for an ideal gas.
flashcards.back: Vertical line on a $p$-$V$ diagram: $W = 0$ (no volume change), so $\Delta U = Q = n C_V \Delta T$. For a monatomic ideal gas, $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$.
flashcards.hint: Isochoric = constant volume $\implies$ zero area under curve.

flashcards.front: Summarize an **isobaric process** ($p = \text{const}$) and Mayer's relation.
flashcards.back: Horizontal line on a $p$-$V$ diagram: $W = p\Delta V = nR\Delta T$ and $Q = n C_P \Delta T$. Applying $\Delta U = Q - W$ gives $C_P - C_V = R$ (so $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R$ for a monatomic gas).
flashcards.hint: Constant pressure needs extra heat $R$ per mole per K to push the piston.

flashcards.front: Summarize an **isothermal process** ($T = \text{const}$) for an ideal gas.
flashcards.back: Slow process along $p = nRT/V$ so temperature stays fixed: $\Delta U = 0$, hence $Q = W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$.
flashcards.hint: Constant $T$ $\implies \Delta U = 0 \implies$ all heat turns into work.

flashcards.front: How is an **adiabatic process** achieved, and what equations govern it?
flashcards.back: No heat flows ($Q = 0$) via thermal insulation or a very rapid process. Thus $\Delta U = -W$, $p_i V_i^\gamma = p_f V_f^\gamma$, and $T_i V_i^{\gamma-1} = T_f V_f^{\gamma-1}$, where $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ ($5/3 \approx 1.67$ for monatomic).
flashcards.hint: Insulated or super fast $\implies Q = 0$, steeper than an isotherm.

flashcards.front: Why is an adiabatic curve steeper than an isotherm on a $p$-$V$ diagram?
flashcards.back: In an adiabatic expansion ($Q = 0$), the gas does work using its internal energy ($\Delta U = -W < 0$), so $T$ drops as $V$ grows; pressure therefore falls faster ($p \propto V^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma > 1$) than at constant $T$ ($p \propto V^{-1}$).
flashcards.hint: Compare $p \propto V^{-\gamma}$ vs. $p \propto V^{-1}$.

flashcards.front: What are the work and efficiency formulas for a cyclic heat engine?
flashcards.back: $W = Q_{\mathrm{h}} - Q_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $e = \frac{W}{Q_{\mathrm{h}}} = 1 - \frac{Q_{\mathrm{c}}}{Q_{\mathrm{h}}}$, where $Q_{\mathrm{h}}$ is heat absorbed from the hot reservoir and $Q_{\mathrm{c}}$ is heat rejected to the cold reservoir.
flashcards.hint: Efficiency = useful work out divided by heat paid in ($Q_{\mathrm{h}}$).

flashcards.front: List the four steps of the **Carnot cycle** in order on a $p$-$V$ diagram.
flashcards.back: $A \to B$: isothermal expansion at $T_{\mathrm{h}}$ (absorbs $Q_{\mathrm{h}}$); $B \to C$: adiabatic expansion ($T_{\mathrm{h}} \to T_{\mathrm{c}}$); $C \to D$: isothermal compression at $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ (rejects $Q_{\mathrm{c}}$); $D \to A$: adiabatic compression ($T_{\mathrm{c}} \to T_{\mathrm{h}}$).
flashcards.hint: Alternating Isothermal–Adiabatic–Isothermal–Adiabatic clockwise loop.

flashcards.front: State **Carnot's Principle** and the Carnot efficiency formula.
flashcards.back: No engine working between two reservoirs at constant temperatures can have a greater efficiency than a reversible engine. Its efficiency is $e = 1 - \frac{T_{\mathrm{c}}}{T_{\mathrm{h}}}$ (temperatures in Kelvin).
flashcards.hint: Reversible = theoretical maximum; always convert temperatures to K.

questions.prompt: A block attached to a horizontal ideal spring oscillates in simple harmonic motion between $x = -A$ and $x = +A$ on a frictionless surface. At the instant the block reaches $x = +A$, which statement about its velocity $v$ and net restoring force $F_x$ is correct?
choices: $v = 0$ and $F_x$ points in the $-x$ direction with maximum magnitude $kA$
$v = 0$ and $F_x = 0$ because the block is momentarily at rest
questions.hint: Use Hooke's law $F_x = -kx$ and remember what happens to velocity at a turning point.
questions.solution: At the positive turning point $x = +A$, the block momentarily stops to reverse direction, so $v = 0$. By Hooke's law, $F_x = -kx = -kA$, so the restoring force has its maximum magnitude $kA$ and points in the $-x$ direction back toward equilibrium ($x = 0$).

questions.prompt: An oscillator completes $25$ full oscillations in $5.0\text{ s}$. What are its period $T$ and angular frequency $\omega$?
questions.hint: First compute linear frequency $f = \text{cycles}/\text{time}$, then find $T = 1/f$ and $\omega = 2\pi f$.
questions.solution: The linear frequency is $f = \frac{25\text{ cycles}}{5.0\text{ s}} = 5.0\text{ Hz}$. The period is $T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{5.0\text{ Hz}} = 0.20\text{ s}$, and the angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(5.0\text{ Hz}) = 10\pi \approx 31.4\text{ rad/s}$.

questions.prompt: A $2.00\text{ kg}$ block on a frictionless horizontal surface is attached to a wall via a spring of force constant $k = 32.00\text{ N/m}$. If the block is pulled to $x = +0.15\text{ m}$ from equilibrium and released from rest at $t = 0$, which equation correctly gives its position $x(t)$?
questions.hint: Compute $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ and check which function satisfies $x(0) = +0.15\text{ m}$ and $v(0) = 0$.
questions.solution: The angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{32.00\text{ N/m}}{2.00\text{ kg}}} = \sqrt{16.0} = 4.00\text{ rad/s}$. Because the block starts from rest at $x(0) = +A = +0.15\text{ m}$, the phase constant is $\phi = 0$, giving $x(t) = (0.15\text{ m})\cos(4.00t)$ (note $v(0) = -A\omega\sin(0) = 0$).

questions.prompt: The position of a particle in simple harmonic motion is given by $x(t) = (0.080\text{ m})\cos\left(5.0t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)$, where $t$ is in seconds. What is the particle's velocity at $t = 0$?
questions.hint: Differentiate $x(t)$ with respect to $t$ using $v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi)$, then evaluate at $t = 0$ in radians.
questions.solution: Differentiating $x(t)$ gives $v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi) = -(0.080\text{ m})(5.0\text{ rad/s})\sin\left(5.0t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -(0.40\text{ m/s})\sin\left(5.0t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)$. At $t = 0$, $v(0) = -0.40\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -0.40\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -0.20\sqrt{3} \approx -0.346\text{ m/s}$.

questions.prompt: A mass $m$ attached to a spring of force constant $k$ oscillates in SHM with period $T = 1.20\text{ s}$. If the mass is replaced by $2m$ and the spring is replaced by a stiffer spring of force constant $8k$, what is the new period $T'$?
questions.hint: Use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ and find the ratio $T'/T$.
questions.solution: The period scales as $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$. Replacing $m \to 2m$ and $k \to 8k$ gives $T' = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2m}{8k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\frac{m}{k}} = \frac{1}{2}T = \frac{1}{2}(1.20\text{ s}) = 0.60\text{ s}$.

questions.prompt: An object oscillates vertically on a spring with $y(t) = A\cos(\omega t)$. Which description correctly matches its position, velocity, and acceleration graphs over time?
choices: When $y = +A$, velocity is $+v_{\max}$ and acceleration is $0$
When $y = 0$ and moving downward, velocity is $-v_{\max}$ and acceleration is $+a_{\max}$
Acceleration is proportional to $+y$, so $a(t)$ has the same sign as $y(t)$ everywhere
When $y = +A$, velocity is $0$ and acceleration is $-a_{\max}$; when $y = 0$, acceleration is $0$ and speed is $v_{\max}$
questions.hint: Check $v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t)$ and $a(t) = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2 y(t)$ at $t = 0$ and $t = T/4$.
questions.solution: With $y(t) = A\cos(\omega t)$, we have $v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t)$ and $a(t) = -\omega^2 y(t)$. At $t = 0$ ($y = +A$), $v = 0$ and $a = -A\omega^2 = -a_{\max}$. At $t = T/4$ ($y = 0$), $a = 0$ and $|v| = A\omega = v_{\max}$.

questions.prompt: A $0.50\text{ kg}$ block attached to a spring with $k = 200\text{ N/m}$ oscillates on a frictionless surface with amplitude $A = 0.10\text{ m}$. What is the speed of the block when its displacement is $x = 0.060\text{ m}$?
questions.hint: Apply conservation of mechanical energy $\frac{1}{2}kx^2 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$ or $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.
questions.solution: Total energy is $E_{\text{Total}} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}(200\text{ N/m})(0.10\text{ m})^2 = 1.00\text{ J}$. At $x = 0.060\text{ m}$, elastic potential energy is $U = \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.060)^2 = 0.36\text{ J}$, so kinetic energy is $K = 1.00 - 0.36 = 0.64\text{ J}$. Thus $\frac{1}{2}(0.50)v^2 = 0.64 \implies v^2 = 2.56 \implies v = 1.60\text{ m/s}$. Equivalently, $\omega = \sqrt{200/0.50} = 20\text{ rad/s}$ and $v = 20\sqrt{0.10^2 - 0.060^2} = 20(0.080) = 1.60\text{ m/s}$.

questions.prompt: In an ideal mass-spring simple harmonic oscillator of amplitude $A$, at what displacement $x$ from equilibrium is the kinetic energy equal to three times the elastic potential energy ($K = 3U$)?
questions.hint: Substitute $K = 3U$ into $E_{\text{Total}} = U + K = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$ to express $U$ as a fraction of $E_{\text{Total}}$.
questions.solution: Since $E_{\text{Total}} = U + K$ and $K = 3U$, we have $E_{\text{Total}} = 4U$, so $U = \frac{1}{4}E_{\text{Total}}$. Setting $\frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}kA^2\right)$ gives $x^2 = \frac{A^2}{4}$, hence $x = \pm\frac{A}{2}$.

questions.prompt: A $0.25\text{ kg}$ block attached to a spring of constant $k = 100\text{ N/m}$ oscillates in SHM on a frictionless track. At a certain instant, the block is at $x = 0.030\text{ m}$ and moving at speed $v = 0.80\text{ m/s}$. What are the oscillation amplitude $A$ and total mechanical energy $E_{\text{Total}}$?
questions.hint: Compute $E_{\text{Total}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ first, then equate it to $\frac{1}{2}kA^2$.

questions.prompt: A simple pendulum having a length of $75.000\text{ cm}$ is measured to have a period of $1.7357\text{ s}$ for small oscillations. What is the acceleration due to gravity $g$ in this region?
questions.hint: Convert $L$ to meters and solve $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ for $g$.
questions.solution: Converting length to SI units gives $L = 0.75000\text{ m}$. From $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, squaring both sides yields $g = \frac{4\pi^2 L}{T^2} = \frac{4\pi^2(0.75000\text{ m})}{(1.7357\text{ s})^2} = \frac{29.6088}{3.01265} \approx 9.8281\text{ m/s}^2 \approx 9.828\text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.prompt: A simple pendulum undergoes small-angle oscillations with angular frequency $\omega$ and period $T$. If the bob mass is doubled ($2m$) and the string length is quadrupled ($4L$), how do $\omega$ and $T$ change?
choices: $\omega$ decreases by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ and $T$ increases by $\sqrt{2}$
$\omega$ is quartered and $T$ increases by a factor of $4$
Both $\omega$ and $T$ remain unchanged because mass increased along with length
questions.hint: Check whether bob mass $m$ appears in $\omega = \sqrt{g/L}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$.
questions.solution: For small oscillations of a simple pendulum, $\omega = \sqrt{g/L}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ are completely independent of bob mass $m$. Quadrupling $L \to 4L$ yields $\omega' = \sqrt{g/(4L)} = \omega/2$ and $T' = 2\pi\sqrt{4L/g} = 2T$.

questions.prompt: To reduce wind-induced swaying of a skyscraper, engineers install a physical pendulum made of a uniform beam of constant density and mass $100\text{ metric tons}$, pivoted at one end ($I = \frac{1}{3}m\ell^2$). If the beam must oscillate at $f = 0.50\text{ Hz}$ (use $g = 9.80\text{ m/s}^2$), what should be the total length $\ell$ of the beam?
questions.hint: Use $\omega = \sqrt{mgL_{\text{CM}}/I}$ where $L_{\text{CM}} = \ell/2$ and $I = \frac{1}{3}m\ell^2$, with $\omega = 2\pi f$.
questions.solution: The required angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(0.50\text{ Hz}) = \pi\text{ rad/s}$. For a uniform beam of length $\ell$ pivoted at one end, the pivot-to-CM distance is $L_{\text{CM}} = \ell/2$ and the moment of inertia is $I = \frac{1}{3}m\ell^2$. Thus $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{mg(\ell/2)}{\frac{1}{3}m\ell^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{3g}{2\ell}}$. Solving for $\ell$ gives $\ell = \frac{3g}{2\omega^2} = \frac{3(9.80)}{2\pi^2} \approx 1.49\text{ m}$ (independent of the $100$-ton mass).

questions.prompt: A uniform rigid rod of length $\ell = 1.20\text{ m}$ is suspended from a frictionless horizontal pivot at one end ($I = \frac{1}{3}m\ell^2$) and undergoes small-angle oscillations. Using $g = 9.80\text{ m/s}^2$, what is its period of oscillation $T$?
questions.hint: Use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgL_{\text{CM}})}$ with $L_{\text{CM}} = \ell/2$.
questions.solution: With $I = \frac{1}{3}m\ell^2$ and pivot-to-CM distance $L_{\text{CM}} = \ell/2$, the physical pendulum period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{3}m\ell^2}{mg(\ell/2)}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2\ell}{3g}}$. Substituting $\ell = 1.20\text{ m}$ and $g = 9.80\text{ m/s}^2$ gives $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2(1.20)}{3(9.80)}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.80}{9.80}} \approx 1.795\text{ s} \approx 1.80\text{ s}$.

questions.prompt: A $0.50\text{ kg}$ mass on a spring oscillates in a viscous fluid with linear damping constant $b = 0.10\text{ kg/s}$ and initial amplitude $A_0 = 0.20\text{ m}$. What is the amplitude envelope $A(t) = A_0 e^{-(b/2m)t}$ at $t = 10.0\text{ s}$?
questions.hint: Compute the exponent $-\frac{b}{2m}t$ carefully, making sure to include the factor of $2$ in $2m$.
questions.solution: The decay constant is $\frac{b}{2m} = \frac{0.10\text{ kg/s}}{2(0.50\text{ kg})} = 0.10\text{ s}^{-1}$. At $t = 10.0\text{ s}$, the exponent is $-0.10(10.0) = -1.0$, so $A(10.0\text{ s}) = 0.20 e^{-1.0} \approx 0.20(0.36788) \approx 0.0736\text{ m}$.

questions.prompt: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ block attached to a spring with $k = 50\text{ N/m}$ experiences a viscous damping force $F_D = -bv$ with $b = 12\text{ kg/s}$. What are its damped angular frequency $\omega$ and the minimum damping constant $b_{\text{crit}}$ required for critical damping?
questions.hint: Use $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m} - \left(\frac{b}{2m}\right)^2}$ and set $b_{\text{crit}}^2 = 4mk$.
questions.solution: First, $\frac{k}{m} = \frac{50}{2.0} = 25\text{ s}^{-2}$ and $\frac{b}{2m} = \frac{12}{2(2.0)} = 3.0\text{ s}^{-1}$. Thus $\omega = \sqrt{25 - (3.0)^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4.0\text{ rad/s}$. Critical damping occurs when $b_{\text{crit}}^2 = 4mk = 4(2.0)(50) = 400$, giving $b_{\text{crit}} = 20\text{ kg/s}$.

questions.prompt: Three identical mass-spring systems are displaced equally from equilibrium and released in fluids with different damping constants $b$. Which condition describes a system that returns to equilibrium as rapidly as possible without crossing $x = 0$ (no oscillation)?
questions.hint: Check the threshold where the damped frequency $\omega = \sqrt{k/m - (b/2m)^2}$ just reaches zero.
questions.solution: When $b^2 < 4mk$, the system is underdamped and oscillates across $x = 0$. When $b^2 > 4mk$, it is overdamped and returns sluggishly without oscillating. At the boundary $b^2 = 4mk$ (critically damped), the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without overshooting or oscillating.

questions.prompt: A damped oscillator with natural frequency $f_0$ is driven by a periodic external force of constant amplitude $F_0$ at varying driving frequency $f$. As the damping constant $b$ is increased from small damping to heavy damping, how does the steady-state resonance curve $A(f)$ change?
choices: The peak amplitude increases and becomes narrower around $f_0$
The peak amplitude decreases and the curve flattens/broadens, eventually losing any peak for heavy damping
The resonance peak remains the same height but shifts to $2f_0$
The oscillator stops moving at $f = f_0$ while oscillating strongly at all other frequencies
questions.hint: Examine $A = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{m^2(\omega^2 - \omega_0^2)^2 + b^2\omega^2}}$ as $b$ grows larger.
questions.solution: At $\omega = \omega_0$, the steady-state amplitude is $A = F_0/(b\omega_0)$, which is inversely proportional to $b$. Increasing damping $b$ lowers the peak amplitude, broadens the response curve, and for heavy damping eliminates the resonance peak altogether.

questions.prompt: A $1.0\text{ kg}$ mass attached to a spring with $k = 25\text{ N/m}$ and damping constant $b = 3.0\text{ kg/s}$ is driven by a sinusoidal force of amplitude $F_0 = 3.0\text{ N}$ at driving angular frequency $\omega = 4.0\text{ rad/s}$. What is the steady-state oscillation amplitude $A$?
questions.hint: Find $\omega_0^2 = k/m$ first, then substitute into $A = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{m^2(\omega^2 - \omega_0^2)^2 + b^2\omega^2}}$.
questions.solution: The undamped natural angular frequency squared is $\omega_0^2 = \frac{k}{m} = \frac{25}{1.0} = 25\text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2$. Substituting $\omega = 4.0\text{ rad/s}$, $m = 1.0\text{ kg}$, $b = 3.0\text{ kg/s}$, and $F_0 = 3.0\text{ N}$ into the steady-state amplitude formula gives $m(\omega^2 - \omega_0^2) = 1.0(16 - 25) = -9.0\text{ N/m}$ and $b\omega = (3.0)(4.0) = 12\text{ N/m}$. Thus the denominator is $\sqrt{(-9.0)^2 + (12)^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15\text{ N/m}$, and $A = \frac{3.0\text{ N}}{15\text{ N/m}} = 0.20\text{ m}$.

questions.prompt: A sinusoidal transverse wave travels in the $+x$-direction along a long horizontal string. Consider a small painted dot on the string at a fixed horizontal position $x_0$. As the wave passes, how does the painted dot move?
choices: It travels continuously in the $+x$-direction at the wave speed $v$.
It oscillates up and down in simple harmonic motion perpendicular to the $+x$-direction with amplitude $A$.
It moves back and forth horizontally parallel to the $+x$-direction with amplitude $A$.
It remains completely motionless while energy passes underneath it.
questions.hint: In a transverse wave, distinguish the motion of the wave pattern from the motion of individual medium elements.
questions.solution: In a transverse wave, the disturbance of the medium is perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. While the wave pattern and energy travel along $+x$ at speed $v$, each mass element on the string (such as the painted dot at $x_0$) oscillates vertically in simple harmonic motion between $+A$ and $-A$.

questions.prompt: Ocean waves pass an offshore buoy with a crest-to-crest distance of $12.0$ m and a vertical crest-to-trough height of $1.80$ m. If the buoy takes $2.50$ s to drop from a wave crest directly to the next trough, what are the wave amplitude $A$ and wave speed $v$?
questions.hint: From crest to trough spans $2A$ vertically and half a period ($T/2$) in time.
questions.solution:
1. The vertical distance from crest ($+A$) to trough ($-A$) is $2A=1.80$ m, so $A = 0.90$ m.
2. Moving from a crest to the very next trough takes half a period: $T/2 = 2.50$ s, which gives $T = 5.00$ s.
3. With wavelength $\lambda = 12.0$ m, the wave speed is $v = \frac{\lambda}{T} = \frac{12.0}{5.00} = 2.40$ m/s.

questions.prompt: A transverse wave on a string is given by $y(x, t) = (0.040\,\text{m})\sin(5.0\pi x + 20\pi t + \frac{\pi}{3})$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds. What are its wavelength $\lambda$, wave speed $v$, and propagation direction?
questions.hint: Match the argument to $kx \mp \omega t + \phi$, then use $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ and $v = \omega/k$.
questions.solution:
Comparing with $y(x,t) = A\sin(kx \mp \omega t + \phi)$ gives $k = 5.0\pi$ rad/m and $\omega = 20\pi$ rad/s.
1. Wavelength: $\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{k} = \frac{2\pi}{5.0\pi} = 0.40$ m.
2. Speed: $v = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{20\pi}{5.0\pi} = 4.0$ m/s.
3. Direction: Setting constant phase $\theta = 5.0\pi x + 20\pi t + \frac{\pi}{3} = \text{const}$ and differentiating with respect to $t$ yields $dx/dt = -\omega/k = -4.0$ m/s, so the wave travels in the $-x$-direction.
